instruction: There's a person who comes in and just writes stuff on a board and leaves. What are they doing?
response: That's probably someone from your care team updating the whiteboard in your room — those boards usually show things like your nurse's name, important goals for the day, and any scheduled tests or visits. It's a way of keeping everyone who comes into your room informed at a glance, including you and your family. If you want to know who that specific person was, look at their badge the next time they come in. You can also ask your nurse: 'Who's the person who updates the board?' They'll tell you exactly.

instruction: Why are there so many different people coming in to see me? How many doctors do I have?
response: At Children's Hospital you might have more people involved in your care than you'd expect — and it can feel like a lot! Depending on your situation, you might have a main doctor, a specialist or two, a resident who checks on you regularly, nurses for each shift, and other team members like a physiotherapist or dietitian. It's not because something is complicated in a scary way — it's because your hospital has experts for lots of different things. If you want to understand who's who, ask your nurse to introduce the main players: 'Can you tell me the names and jobs of the main people looking after me?'

instruction: The person who brought my lunch wasn't wearing the same colour as the nurses. Who are they?
response: That person is from the food services team — they work in the hospital kitchen and deliver meals to patients. They're an important part of the team even though they're not medical staff. They usually wear a different uniform colour to distinguish their role. If you have a question about your food — like if something doesn't look right or you want something different — you can mention it to them directly or tell your nurse, who can pass along any food preferences or dietary needs to the kitchen team.

instruction: There's someone who walked around with a dog today. Is that their pet or a hospital dog?
response: That's a therapy dog! Children's Hospital has certified therapy dogs who visit patients to provide comfort and a little bit of home. They're brought in by their handlers from programs like St. John Ambulance and go through special training to be calm and gentle around hospital environments. They're not the handler's pet in the regular sense — their job is to visit kids like you. If you'd love a visit from one of the therapy dogs, ask your nurse — they can often arrange for a visit to your room. Lots of kids find it really cheering.

instruction: A person asked me how I was feeling but they weren't a nurse. They had a different badge. Who was that?
response: It might have been a Child Life specialist! They're a special part of the team at Children's Hospital whose job is specifically about how kids are feeling emotionally — not medically. They help kids understand what's happening, deal with scary feelings, and find ways to feel more comfortable and less bored. They're not there to do anything medical at all. If you liked talking to that person and want to see them again, just mention it to your nurse: 'Can the Child Life specialist come back?' They'll arrange it.

instruction: Sometimes there's a group of people who all come in together and talk about me. Who are all those people?
response: That's called a ward round or care round — the group is your medical team checking in together. It usually includes your main doctor, one or more residents or students who are learning, sometimes a pharmacist, and possibly other specialists. They talk through how you're doing and what the plan is for the day. You're allowed to be part of that conversation and ask questions while they're in the room. If it feels confusing to have so many people at once, you can ask your nurse afterward to explain what was discussed in plainer language.

instruction: Is there someone I can call if I need something and my nurse is busy?
response: Yes — the call button next to your bed alerts the nurses' station right away, and even if your specific nurse is occupied with someone else, another member of the nursing team will come to check on you. You're never on your own waiting for just one person. Press the button whenever you need something — it doesn't have to be an emergency. That's what it's there for.

instruction: The person who gave me my medicine this morning looks really young. Are they still learning?
response: They might be a student nurse, a nursing student doing their clinical placement, or a young-looking qualified nurse — it's hard to tell from appearance alone. Nursing students always work under the supervision of a fully qualified nurse, who is responsible for your care. If you're ever unsure who someone is or what their training level is, you're allowed to ask: 'Are you a student or a qualified nurse?' They'll tell you honestly. Your safety is the most important thing, and everything that happens with your care is checked and supervised.

instruction: There's a room down the hall with toys and a person who plays games. Can I go there?
response: That sounds like the playroom or activity room, and the person there is probably a Child Life specialist or recreation therapist — their job is to help kids have fun and feel more normal while they're in hospital. Many kids can visit if their care team says it's okay for them to walk around. Ask your nurse: 'Am I allowed to go to the playroom down the hall?' They'll check what your current plan says and either give you the go-ahead or, if you can't go right now, might be able to arrange for someone from that room to come to you.

instruction: What's a physiotherapist? One is coming to see me tomorrow and I don't know what they do.
response: A physiotherapist — sometimes called a physio or PT — is a specialist who helps people move their bodies well. They're experts in muscles, joints, movement, and recovery. Depending on why you're in hospital, they might help you strengthen muscles, improve balance, learn how to move safely while you're healing, or just get up and walk around when you haven't been moving for a while. Their visits are often one of the more active and hands-on parts of hospital care. They'll explain exactly what they want to do before they do it, and you can always ask questions during the visit.

instruction: There have been three different doctors who've come in separately and said slightly different things. Who's actually in charge of my care?
response: That's a fair question and a sign you need clearer communication. In a hospital like LHSC, you typically have an attending physician who is the responsible physician for your overall care — they're the one accountable for your treatment plan. The others might be specialists, residents, or fellows, each focusing on a specific aspect. Ask your nurse or the next doctor who comes in: 'Who is the most responsible physician for my care?' That person should be the one giving you the bottom line. If information from different people seems contradictory, it's also fair to ask for a team meeting so you're getting one consistent message.

instruction: Someone called a 'social worker' wants to meet with me. What are they actually there for?
response: A hospital social worker works with patients and families on non-medical aspects of care — things like emotional support, family dynamics, financial stress, housing, school, discharge planning, and connecting you with community resources. They're not there because something is wrong with how you're coping; they're part of routine care for many patients, especially those with longer stays. You can talk to them about things that have nothing to do with your medical diagnosis — like how the experience is affecting your mental health, your relationships, or practical concerns about what happens when you go home. The conversation is confidential within professional limits.

instruction: What's the difference between a specialist and a consultant — are those the same thing?
response: In Canadian hospital practice, the terms are often used interchangeably. A specialist is a physician who has done additional training in a specific area of medicine — cardiology, oncology, neurology, and so on. When they're 'consulted' on your case by your primary team, they're called in as a consultant. So a consultant is a specialist being asked for their expert input. If a consultant comes to see you, they're usually focused on one specific aspect of your care, not your overall situation. Your most responsible physician is still the one overseeing everything.

instruction: There was a person who sat with me for an hour and just talked. They weren't a doctor. What was their role?
response: That sounds like a Child Life specialist, a social worker, or possibly a chaplain or spiritual care provider — all of whom offer support that isn't clinical in the medical sense. Child Life specialists focus on emotional wellbeing and coping for patients of all ages, including teens. They're specifically trained to just be present and supportive without an agenda. If you found that helpful and want to see them again, ask your nurse who came to see you — they'll be able to look it up and arrange another visit. Knowing who it was also lets you ask for them by name next time.

instruction: I want to talk to someone about how all of this is affecting me mentally, not physically. Who do I ask for?
response: Ask your nurse or doctor for a referral to the social work or psychology team — most paediatric hospitals have both. A social worker can provide immediate support and connect you with resources. A psychologist or psychiatrist can provide more structured mental health support if that's what's needed. You can also ask for a Child Life specialist, who works with teens specifically on the emotional side of hospitalization. You don't need to be in crisis to ask for this — ongoing stress, anxiety, low mood, or just needing someone to talk to are all valid reasons. Asking for mental health support is taking your recovery seriously.

instruction: Can I request a specific nurse if I felt more comfortable with one of them?
response: You can make the request, yes. Speak to the charge nurse on your unit — they're the one who does the scheduling. Explain that you felt particularly comfortable with a specific nurse and ask if they can be assigned to you when they're working. This isn't always possible (nurses work specific shifts, units have complex staffing) but it's a reasonable request and many units try to accommodate it. Even if you can't always have that nurse, knowing there's someone you connect with can make the other shifts easier. It's worth asking.

instruction: Who's actually responsible for making sure all the different departments treating me are on the same page?
response: Formally, that's the most responsible physician — usually an attending physician or in some cases a hospitalist — whose job includes coordinating the overall care plan across specialties. In practice, the coordination between departments can have gaps, which is why it matters for you and your family to be active participants. Ask at each visit: 'Has this been shared with my other team?' and at rounds: 'Is everyone aligned on the plan?' If you feel like important information is getting lost between departments, raise it with your care team or ask for a case conference where all the relevant people get together. Patient Relations can also help if coordination is genuinely falling short.

instruction: What's the role of the person who came to talk to me about going home and what happens after?
response: That's likely a discharge planner or a member of the care coordination or transitions team. Their job is specifically to plan what happens when you leave the hospital — making sure you have what you need at home, that follow-up appointments are booked, that any home care or equipment is arranged, and that you and your family understand what to do. It's one of the most important conversations you'll have because what happens in the first days and weeks after discharge significantly affects your recovery. If you have specific concerns about going home — support at home, getting back to school, physical limitations — that person is the right one to raise them with.

instruction: I've been dealing with a lot of different people. Is there one main person I should be directing my questions to?
response: For medical questions — diagnosis, treatment, prognosis, procedures — the most responsible physician is your main point of contact. For day-to-day needs and coordination, your bedside nurse is usually the most responsive. For anything about emotions, coping, or practical life issues, the social worker or Child Life specialist. For problems with how things are being handled, Patient Relations. The system isn't perfectly streamlined, but knowing those four lanes helps. You can also ask your nurse: 'Who's the best person to ask about X?' and they'll usually route you correctly. You don't have to figure out the org chart on your own.

instruction: A medical student asked if they could observe my examination. Did I have to say yes?
response: No. Participating in the education of medical students is voluntary. You have the right to decline, and doing so will not affect the quality of your care in any way. If you said yes and now feel uncomfortable, you can change your mind at any time. If saying no directly feels awkward, you can simply say 'I'd prefer not to have observers today' and leave it at that — you don't owe an explanation. Some people are comfortable being part of teaching; some aren't. Both are completely valid.
